newsitem.title: CANADA: Ag Canada pays C$6 mln for unharvested grain.
newsitem.headline: Ag Canada pays C$6 mln for unharvested grain.

text.p: Agriculture Canada paid out C$6 million in emergency funds to Prairie farmers who were not able to harvest their wheat and barley crops this fall.

"We've issued 750 emergency advances for unthreshed grain for C$6 million and we're forecasting that's probably half the applications we'll be getting," Ag Canada's manager of The Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act Bob Smith said.
The western Prairie harvest was hampered by cold, wet conditions and earlier than normal snowfall in October.
About 1.2 million acres of wheat and barley were not harvested, Smith said.
The emergency funds approved by Canada's federal Parliament November 18 apply only to unharvested as well as damp and tough grain, and only to wheat and barley.
"There's also grain drying advances. We've issued, as of December 12, C$101,000 on 39 applications," Smith said.
Maximum government emergency payments for unthreshed grain is C$15,000 and C$3,000 to dry damp and tough grain.
Two-thirds of low grade No3 Canada Western Red Spring milling wheat is tough and damp, the CWB said.
Canada's elevator system cannot handle all of the tough grain stored on farms due to limited port drying capabilities.
Delivery of tough or damp No3 CWRS wheat may be restricted by its large volume, the CWB added.
Estimates of tonnage or the percentage of the crop were not available.
A C$7 a tonne discount will be applied to the 1996/97 (Aug/July) CWB initial payment for the cost of drying tough wheat at terminal elevators while the actual cost is C$9.75 a tonne, the CWB said.
A C$14.50 a tonne discount will be applied to the initial payment for drying damp wheat while the real cost is C$12.65 a tonne.

Canada's federal government set the initial payment, a government-backed first payment representing 70 to 80 percent of the forecast world price, on July 29 at C$190 a tonne for No1 CWRS, in-store Vancouver or St. Lawrence.
There is also the cost of shrinkage, the loss of weight after drying, the CWB added.
About 2.165 million acres of all crops remained to be harvested in the western Prairies, Alberta and Saskatchewan's agriculture departments said.
